newsitem.title: USA: NOW calls VMI's stance on women "vindictive".
newsitem.headline: NOW calls VMI's stance on women "vindictive".

text.p: Virginia Military Institute is being vindictive in its unbending response to a court order that the historically all-male academy must admit women, the National Organisation for Women said on Tuesday.

School superintendent Gen. Josiah Bunting had said few accommodations would be made for women at the Lexington, Virginia campus: they will have the same "buzz" hair cuts as male cadets, will live in barracks and while they will have their own showers there will be no locks on the doors.

"Basically, we feel that it's vindictive, it's lacking leadership on the part of the board of VMI," Karen Johnson, a NOW vice president and a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel, told Reuters by telephone.
"They want to create a hostile environment, they want to discourage women from applying," Johnson said.

VMI, the last state-supported military academy in the United States to bar women, reluctantly decided on Saturday to admit women after 157 years as an all-male school, following a Supreme Court ruling that said VMI must allow women to attend or forfeit its government funding.
Johnson found the hair requirement inconsistent with policy at the U.S. military service academies, which allow women cadets to keep their hair at a three-inch length.
"The military academies ... have built great teams and created great leaders, and they've done that in spite of the fact that women have longer hair than men in boot training," Johnson said.
As for the lockless doors expected at VMI, Johnson said: "In an ideal world, none of us would have locks on our doors, but it's not an ideal world."

VMI, founded in 1839, was the only state-supported college in the country that had yet to admit women. The institute had said women would be unable to withstand its tough mental and physical training known as "the Rat Line".
The Citadel, the only other state-supported U.S. military academy, admitted females in September after the high court's ruling in the VMI case.
